source.title: Audits Under Resource, Data, and Access Constraints: Scaling Laws For Less Discriminatory Alternatives
source.authors: Sarah H. Cen; S. Goyal; Zaynah Javed; A. Karthik; Percy Liang; Daniel E. Ho

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports synthetic-model experiments on scaling loss-fairness Pareto frontiers and shows that fitted exponents and curves can vary with fitting choices and setup. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims, but it does not test language-model pretraining loss laws directly.
record.gate_note: The study’s own experiments are on synthetic supervised binary-classification MLPs, measuring BCE loss along demographic-parity Pareto frontiers—not held-out language-model pretraining loss. The paper cites language-model scaling-law work and adopts a parameter/data scaling form for its frontier; cited results are not this study’s results. The formula-shape illustrations in Figures 3–5 are simulations of the expression, not trained-model outcomes. Procedures and numbers proposed for fitting a frontier, including the suggestion that seven models may suffice, are not empirical results.
record.test_reason: The study's main object is a loss-fairness Pareto frontier, not a standalone loss law. It does train four synthetic-data MLP classifiers (8,080 to 423,040 parameters, data fixed) and reports that the frontier's loss intercept B scales as a power of N plus a constant. That is a new-setting result for V5: supervised tabular classification. It also reports several hand-chosen fits to the same data with different exponents, which bears on V7. It does not test language-model pretraining loss (V1–V4) or downstream tasks (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude their closed-form upper bound serves as a scaling law for loss-fairness frontiers. Synthetic experiments, varying only model size, corroborate it: the intercept scales as N^-α plus a constant, and frontiers follow the predicted shape even with X dependent on A. They acknowledge the fits are imperfect and non-unique and the experiments small-scale. They leave real data, larger scale and uncertainty quantification to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments train synthetic-data MLP binary classifiers with BCE plus a demographic-parity regularizer, vary the regularization weight, and fit a loss-fairness frontier. They do not reproduce the language-model pretraining measurements or compute-optimal allocation methods of the cited original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted curves are reported to be non-unique; the selected fit and parameter-count exponent vary. The experiments also vary synthetic settings π and ζ. The main model-scaling test holds D constant and varies model size; frontier tracing uses linear scalarization and varies the regularization weight.

fits_no_version.finding: The empirical BCE-loss vs demographic-parity-gap Pareto frontiers of synthetic MLPs follow the paper's closed-form frontier shape. The fit is good but imperfect, including when X and A are dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-fairness Pareto frontiers follow a closed-form shape whose only scale-dependent term is an additive loss offset.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (venue in supplied metadata); paper text labels it a preprint under review.
record.problems: Experiments are small-scale and synthetic, with no real-data or language-model pretraining evaluation. The main scaling experiment varies model size while holding data size constant. The empirical frontier is acknowledged to be imperfect, and multiple fits can match the curves. Training uses three random trials per configuration, but no confidence intervals or other quantified uncertainty for the scaling results are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the individual curve points in Figures 6 and 10–13: the paper gives no tabulated point values, and the relevant textual results summarize the scaling sweeps and fits. Figure-only visual values were not transcribed. Figures 3–5 and Appendix E Figures 7–9 illustrate formula shapes rather than outcomes from trained models.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No quantitative extrapolation test. The Figure 11/13 fits are tuned on the small model and shown against larger ones without error metrics, and the span is under two orders of magnitude.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.

Only synthetic 20-dimensional tabular binary classification with parameter scaling at fixed data. No data-size scaling, other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. Only four sizes, under two orders of magnitude.
Parameter counting, training schedule, data choices and compute-optimal split are not varied. Curve bending away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: The authors state the typical N^-0.5 exponent did not fit their results well, so per-figure exponents were used. This bears on how stable the exponent is.
No numeric intercept-B values, fit residuals or goodness-of-fit numbers per model size; the power-law claim for B is textual only.

record.verdict_notes: r3 and r4 are the same fit; the Figure 6 caption reports products of the constants. All scaling evidence comes from four tiny MLPs on synthetic data. The power-law form for B is borrowed from LM literature rather than independently established. The authors do not report how the exponents in r3–r7 were fitted; the captions describe some fits as chosen by hand to lower-bound the larger models.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model pretraining loss sweep against parameter count, training tokens, or compute; the experiments measure BCE on synthetic supervised classifiers and their loss-fairness frontiers.
No test that small-run fits predict language-model runs orders of magnitude larger. The synthetic MLP size sweep spans 8,080 to 423,040 parameters and concerns frontier curves.
No comparison of parameter/token allocations under fixed compute, and no compute-optimal allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.

Tests synthetic supervised binary classification and loss-fairness frontiers only. Does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or whether the same form applies to standalone held-out pretraining loss.
No downstream-task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss is measured.

Reports sensitivity of fitted frontier parameters/exponents to fit choice and synthetic setup. Does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules as a varied factor, language-model training data, or compute-optimal parameter/token splits.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLPs ([80, 80], [160, 160], [320, 320], and [640, 640] hidden units)
rows.operation_detail: Compared empirical BCE-loss/demographic-parity Pareto frontiers across model sizes and fitted the Theorem 4.3 frontier form; training data size was held constant for the model-scaling test.

conditions.value: Synthetic 20-dimensional data; same distribution for train and test
Model size varied; D held constant

rows.measure: Empirical held-out BCE-loss versus demographic-parity-gap Pareto frontier and its fit by the proposed closed-form frontier
rows.value: The fitted curve mimics the empirical frontiers well, though imperfectly; the authors report that the empirical frontiers follow the closed-form shape.
rows.note: This is an aggregate textual assessment of the four-size sweep; Figure 6 plots the sizes separately. It is a synthetic supervised-classification frontier result, not a language-model pretraining-loss result.
rows.check: Measures how well the paper's closed-form loss-vs-fairness-gap frontier shape fits, not whether loss follows a power law in scale. It belongs under fits_no_version, not V5.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Examined how the loss-intercept term B of the fitted loss-fairness frontier changes with model size.

conditions.value: Model size varied; D held constant

rows.measure: Scaling of the frontier’s y-intercept B
rows.value: The y-intercepts nearly perfectly scale proportionally to N^-α + D^-β; the Figure 6 fit uses 55(N^-0.7 + D^-0.5).
rows.note: This reports scaling of a term in the loss-fairness frontier, not a general standalone loss law.
rows.check: The state rests only on the authors' words ('nearly perfectly scales'); no intercept values are tabulated. Only N varies, over about 1.7 orders of magnitude. D is held constant, so the D term and its 0.5 exponent are assumed, not estimated.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Reported one fit of the proposed frontier form to the empirical curves.
rows.measure: Fitted frontier parameters and parameter-count exponent
rows.note: The paper reports multiple possible fits to the same empirical frontier; this is one of them.
rows.check: Duplicates the r4 fit. The Figure 6 caption's 'c=0.0176, c′=0.92, c′′=0.1424' are reparameterised products: 0.16×0.11=0.0176, 0.16×0.89=0.1424, and 0.92 is C7. Same exponent 0.7, C2=55 and bias −0.285 as Figure 10. Treat r3 and r4 as one fit, not two independent ones.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Reported an alternative fit of the proposed frontier form to the empirical curves.
rows.measure: Fitted frontier parameters and parameter-count exponent
rows.note: Another fit for the same π=0.2, ζ=0.5 setting; the caption says the curve mimics the empirical data well though imperfectly.
rows.check: Same fit as r3 (see r3). Its value matters only when compared with r5's alternative fit on the same data.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Reported an intentionally chosen alternative fit that fits the small-model curve and extrapolates to larger models.

conditions.value: Figure 11 fit; intentionally chosen to lower-bound larger models

rows.measure: Fitted frontier parameters and parameter-count exponent
rows.note: The authors say the fit is intentionally selected to lower-bound larger models and that multiple fits are possible.
rows.check: Hand-chosen fit made to lower-bound the larger models. Against r4 on identical data: exponent 0.8 vs 0.7, C2 150 vs 55, bias −1.205 vs −0.285.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Reported a fit of the frontier form for a second synthetic setting.
rows.measure: Fitted frontier parameters and parameter-count exponent
rows.note: The caption describes the fit as mimicking the empirical data well but imperfectly.
rows.check: Exponent 0.5 in the second setting (π=0.4, ζ=2), versus 0.7–0.8 in the first. Shows the exponent shifts with the data-generating setting.

rows.subject: Synthetic MLP scaling sweep
rows.operation_detail: Reported an alternative, intentionally chosen fit for the second synthetic setting.

conditions.value: Figure 13 fit; intentionally chosen to lower-bound larger models

rows.measure: Fitted frontier parameters and parameter-count exponent
rows.note: The caption reports this as an alternative fit chosen to lower-bound larger models. It contains an apparent inconsistency in the stated C7 values, reproduced as given.
rows.check: Alternative fit on the same data as r6, with exponent 0.8 vs 0.5. The caption has a typo ('c′ = C6 = C7 = 0.5' alongside C7=0.82).

relationships.condition: Synthetic-data MLP binary classifiers, 8k–423k parameters, D held constant, π=0.2/ζ=0.5 and π=0.4/ζ=2
relationships.reason: The authors state the frontier's loss intercept scales nearly perfectly as N^-α plus a constant (r2). This is weak support: textual, four sizes, exponent fitted by hand.
relationships.display_finding: The frontier loss intercept reportedly followed N^−α plus a constant nearly perfectly across four sizes, with the exponent fitted by hand.

relationships.reason: The fitted N exponent is 0.7–0.8 at π=0.2 and 0.5–0.8 at π=0.4 (r4–r7). The authors note the typical N^-0.5 did not fit well, so the exponent is setting-specific here.
relationships.display_finding: Fitted N exponents were 0.7–0.8 at π = 0.2 and 0.5–0.8 at π = 0.4, while N^-0.5 fit poorly.

relationships.condition: Same empirical frontiers fitted twice: fit as closely as possible vs fit to lower-bound larger models
relationships.reason: Identical data give exponents 0.7 vs 0.8 (r4 vs r5) and 0.5 vs 0.8 (r6 vs r7), with C2 and bias also shifting. The authors say many fits are possible depending on choice.
relationships.display_finding: Changing the fitting objective yields exponents of 0.7 versus 0.8 and 0.5 versus 0.8 on identical data, while C2 and bias also shift.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic supervised binary-classification MLPs; tested model-size sweeps and reported frontier fits
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that the synthetic loss-fairness frontiers follow the proposed form and that the fitted form tracks them well, though imperfectly (r1–r2). This is limited evidence for the frontier form in this synthetic regime, not a general pretraining-loss law.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported fit choices for the synthetic settings π=0.2, ζ=0.5 and π=0.4, ζ=2
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports multiple possible fits, including different parameter-count exponents (0.7 versus 0.8) and different fitted constants for the same or related frontier data (r3–r7).
